title: U.S. House · California's 46th District
area: North-central Orange County, including Anaheim, Santa Ana, Orange and Garden Grove. Redrawn under Proposition 50 (approved November 2025).

context.text: Incumbent Lou Correa (D) and Republican David Pan advanced from the June 2, 2026 top-two primary, defeating two other Democratic candidates and a Democratic write-in candidate.

candidates.name: Lou Correa
candidates.ballotNote: Advanced from the June 2, 2026 top-two primary.

summary.text: Lou Correa is the Democratic incumbent in the 46th District, which covers Orange County cities including Anaheim and Santa Ana, and has served in the U.S. House since 2016. Before Congress he held office in the California State Assembly, on the Orange County Board of Supervisors and in the California State Senate. His campaign website describes him as the son of working-class parents who has served Orange County since 1998.

background.text: Born in East Los Angeles; after his mother's death the family spent several years in Zacatecas, Mexico, before he and his father settled in the Penguin City neighborhood of Anaheim, where he began second grade speaking only Spanish.
Graduated from Anaheim High School and earned a B.A. in economics from California State University, Fullerton in 1980, and an MBA and Juris Doctor from UCLA in 1985.
Worked as a teacher in the Rancho Santiago Community College District, and as an investment banker and real estate broker.

Lost a 1996 race for the California State Assembly to the Republican incumbent by 93 votes, then won the seat in a 1998 rematch; he served in the Assembly from 1998 to 2004, chairing the Business and Professions Committee and the Public Employees, Retirement and Social Security Committee among others, until term limits ended his service.

Elected to the Orange County Board of Supervisors in 2004, becoming the first Democrat on the board since 1987, and represented the first supervisorial district, which includes Garden Grove, Santa Ana and Westminster, until 2006.

Served in the California State Senate from 2006 to 2014, winning the 34th District seat in 2006 and re-election in 2010; in a January 2015 special election he lost a race for the Orange County Board of Supervisors by 43 votes.

Elected to the U.S. House in 2016 to the 46th District seat vacated by Loretta Sanchez, who ran for U.S. Senate, after finishing first in the June primary and winning the general election with 69.9% of the vote.

Serves on the House Homeland Security Committee, where he is ranking member of the Subcommittee on Border Security and Enforcement, and on the Judiciary Committee; he is a member of the New Democrat Coalition and the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.
In July 2024 he was named one of six Democratic members of a bipartisan House task force investigating the attempted assassination of Donald Trump.

priorities.text: Ensuring everyone has access to affordable and quality healthcare, which he calls one of his top priorities.
priorities.quote: Ensuring everyone has access to affordable and quality healthcare is one of Congressman Correa’s top priorities.

priorities.text: Helping businesses and workers get their fair share, saying the path to the middle class starts with a good job.
priorities.quote: Congressman Correa understands that the path to the middle class starts with a good job.

priorities.text: Continuing to advocate for comprehensive immigration reform.
priorities.quote: Congressman Correa continues to advocate for comprehensive immigration reform.

positions.summary: Opposed repealing the Affordable Care Act and has opposed cuts to Medicaid and Medicare, calling for bipartisan solutions to improve the ACA.
positions.quote: As a Member of Congress, he opposed the repeal of the Affordable Care Act because it would have left 22 million Americans without healthcare coverage.

positions.summary: Has supported legislation to protect police officers and give them access to resources to better protect the communities they serve.
positions.quote: he has supported legislation to protect officers and help them get access to the resources they need to better protect the communities they serve

record.text: Serves on the House Committee on Homeland Security (Border Security and Enforcement, and Counterterrorism and Intelligence subcommittees) and the Committee on the Judiciary (Immigration Integrity, Security, and Enforcement Subcommittee) for the 2025-2026 term.

candidates.researchNotes: His campaign website did not return current content and no 2026 Candidate Connection survey was found, but his official House website's issues page (correa.house.gov/about/issues) was reachable and provided sourced priorities and positions.

candidates.name: David Pan
candidates.ballotNote: Advanced from the June 2, 2026 top-two primary.

summary.text: David Pan is the Republican candidate in the 46th District. He is a professor of German at UC Irvine, has worked as a management consultant at McKinsey and Company, and served on a U.S. State Department commission from 2019 to 2020. He also ran for this seat in 2024, losing to Rep. Lou Correa. He says he is running because of what he sees as the education establishment moving away from merit and equality of opportunity.

background.text: According to his campaign website, he was born and raised in the Chicago area in the 1960s to parents who immigrated from Taiwan, and attended public schools in Chicago and Mount Prospect, Illinois.
Earned an undergraduate degree from Stanford University and a graduate degree from Columbia University.
Has worked at Washington University in St. Louis, Stanford University and Pennsylvania State University, and since 2006 has been a professor of German at UC Irvine.
Worked as a management consultant at McKinsey and Company in Los Angeles.
According to his campaign website, he has been editor of the journal Telos.
According to his campaign website, he served as a commissioner on the U.S. State Department's Commission on Unalienable Rights from 2019 to 2020.
Ran as the Republican nominee for the 46th District in 2024, advancing from the March primary alongside Correa and losing the November general election.

priorities.text: Public safety, saying more police recruitment and law enforcement are needed to make streets safe.
Reducing inflation and the national debt by reducing the size and reach of government.
Securing the border and developing a consistent immigration policy.

positions.summary: Says parents should have the information and access needed to choose among all educational options available in their community.
Says rising crime is endangering families and neighborhoods, and calls for recruiting more police and enforcing laws to make streets safe again.
